title: Scripture speaks to us as we speak to children
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ μετὰ ταῦτα μὴ νοήσας τὰς περὶ θεοῦ ὡς ἀνθρωποπαθοῦς ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς λέξεις διασύρει ὁ Κέλσος ἐν αἷς ὀργῆς λέγονται κατὰ τῶν ἀσεβῶν φωναὶ καὶ ἀπειλαὶ κατὰ τῶν ἡμαρτηκότων, λεκτέον ὅτι, ὥσπερ ἡμεῖς τοῖς κομιδῇ νηπίοις διαλεγόμενοι οὐ τοῦ ἑαυτῶν ἐν τῷ λέγειν στοχαζόμεθα δυνατοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ἁρμοζόμενοι πρὸς τὸ ἀσθενὲς τῶν ὑποκειμένων φαμὲν ταῦτα ἀλλὰ καὶ ποιοῦμεν ἃ φαίνεται ἡμῖν χρήσιμα εἰς τὴν τῶν παίδων ὡς παίδων ἐπιστροφὴν καὶ διόρθωσιν· οὕτως ἔοικεν ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος ᾠκονομηκέναι τὰ ἀναγεγραμμένα, μετρήσας τῇ δυνάμει τῶν ἀκουόντων καὶ τῷ πρὸς αὐτοὺς χρησίμῳ τὸ ἐν τῇ ἀπαγγελίᾳ πρέπον, καὶ καθόλου γε περὶ τοῦ τοιούτου τρόπου τῆς ἀπαγγελίας τῶν περὶ θεοῦ ἐν τῷ Δευτερονομίῳ οὕτω λέλεκται· „ἐτροποφόρησέ σε κύριος ὁ θεός σου, ὡς εἴ τις τροποφορήσαι ἄνθρωπος τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ.“ οἱονεὶ ἀνθρώπου τρόπους πρὸς τὸ ἀνθρώποις λυσιτελὲς φορῶν ὁ λόγος τοιαῦτα λέγει· οὐ γὰρ ἐδέοντο οἱ πολλοὶ προσωποποιοῦντος θεοῦ ἁρμοζόντως ἑαυτῷ τὰ πρὸς τοὺς τοιούσδε λεχθησόμενα. ἀλλ᾿ ᾧ μέλει τῆς τῶν θείων γραμμάτων σαφηνείας εὑρήσει ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν τὰ λεγόμενα πνευματικὰ τοῖς ὀνομαζομένοις πνευματικοῖς. συγκρίνων τὸ βούλημα τῶν τε πρὸς τοὺς ἀσθενετέρους λεγομένων καὶ τῶν τοῖς ἐντρεχεστέροις ἀπαγγελλομένων, πολλάκις ἐν τῇ αὐτῇ λέξει ἑκατέρων τῷ εἰδότι ἀκούειν αὐτῆς κειμένων.
pass_a_gloss: Since after these, not having understood (νοέω) the expressions (λέξεις) in the Scriptures (γραφαί) about God as having human passions (ἀνθρωποπαθής), Celsus disparages (διασύρω) those in which utterances (φωναί) of wrath (ὀργή) are said against the ungodly (ἀσεβεῖς) and threats (ἀπειλαί) against those who have sinned, it must be said that, just as we, conversing (διαλέγομαι) with quite young infants (νήπιοι), do not aim (στοχάζομαι) in speaking at our own capacity (τὸ δυνατόν), but adapting (ἁρμόζω) to the weakness (τὸ ἀσθενές) of those set under us we say these things, and also do what appears useful to us for the turning (ἐπιστροφή) and correction (διόρθωσις) of the children as children, so the Word of God (ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος) seems to have arranged (οἰκονομέω) the things written down (ἀναγράφω), having measured (μετρέω) by the power (δύναμις) of the hearers and by what is useful to them what is fitting (τὸ πρέπον) in the announcing (ἀπαγγελία). And generally about such a manner (τρόπος) of announcing things about God, in Deuteronomy it has been said thus: the Lord your God bore your ways (τροποφορέω), as if a man would bear the ways of his son (υἱός). As it were bearing (φορέω) the ways (τρόποι) of a man for what profits (λυσιτελής) men, the Word says such things; for the many (οἱ πολλοί) did not need God represented as speaking (προσωποποιέω), fittingly to himself, the things to be said to such people. But one who cares (μέλει) for the clarity (σαφήνεια) of the divine letters (θεῖα γράμματα) will find from them the things called spiritual (πνευματικά) for those named spiritual (πνευματικοί), comparing (συγκρίνω) the intent (βούλημα) of the things said to the weaker (ἀσθενέστεροι) and of those announced to the more skilled (ἐντρεχέστεροι), often both lying in the same expression for one who knows how to hear (ἀκούω) it.
pass_b_english: After this Celsus, failing to understand them, ridicules the passages in the Scriptures that speak of God as though he were subject to human passions, the passages in which words of wrath are spoken against the ungodly and threats against those who have sinned. To this we must say: just as we, when we talk with very young children, do not aim in our speech at the full measure of our own ability, but adapt ourselves to the weakness of those in our charge and say, and also do, what seems to us useful for turning the children back and correcting them, as children, so the Word of God seems to have arranged what has been written, measuring what was fitting in the telling by the capacity of the hearers and by what would be useful to them.

And in general, about this manner of speaking of God, it is said in Deuteronomy: “The Lord your God bore your ways, as a man might bear the ways of his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31). Bearing, as it were, the ways of a man for the benefit of human beings, the Word says such things. For the many did not need God, where he is represented as speaking, to say what was to be said to such people in a way befitting himself.

But whoever cares about the clear meaning of the divine writings will find from them the things that are called spiritual for those who are called spiritual (1 Corinthians 2:13), comparing the intent of what is said to the weaker with that of what is announced to the more advanced, since both often lie in the same expression for anyone who knows how to hear it.

choices.choice: sense fixed: the ridiculed passages are the same passages Celsus misunderstands, not a subset ('pulls apart those in which' made 'ridicules the passages ..., the passages in which')
'say these things and also do what seems to us useful' made 'say, and also do, what seems to us useful' (ταῦτα ... ἅ is one object of both verbs)
'for turning and correcting the children as children' made 'for turning the children back and correcting them, as children'
'As if bearing the ways of a man for what profits human beings' smoothed to 'Bearing, as it were, the ways of a man for the benefit of human beings'
Deuteronomy 1:31 (LXX ἐτροποφόρησε) and 1 Corinthians 2:13 checked against the verses

Deuteronomy 1:31: Origen reads ἐτροποφόρησε (‘bore your ways’, put up with your manners), not the variant ἐτροφοφόρησε (‘carried you as a nurse’); his next sentence builds on τρόπους (‘ways’), so ‘bore your ways’ is kept in both places to show the link. ‘ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος’ and ‘ὁ λόγος’ could mean either the divine Word or the scriptural word; for Origen the Word is the speaker in Scripture, so ‘the Word’ is capitalised; this is an interpretive choice. ‘προσωποποιοῦντος θεοῦ’ = God represented as speaking in person. ‘πνευματικὰ τοῖς … πνευματικοῖς … συγκρίνων’ clearly echoes 1 Corinthians 2:13 (‘πνευματικοῖς πνευματικὰ συγκρίνοντες’), so it is cited inline. ‘διασύρει’ rendered ‘ridicules’; the passages he ridicules are the same ones he fails to understand (the relative ἐν αἷς describes them, it does not pick out a subset).
